extracted.intended_audience: newspaper editors, reporters and general readers following breaking international/war news
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting and editorial guidance for covering the German invasions of Norway and Denmark (breaking international/war news), including suggested insertions, chronology, official communiques, eyewitness/diplomatic dispatches, strategic background, and human-interest details.

rubrics_metrics.name: EDITORS: TO COVER DEVELOPMENTS THE FOLLOWING MAY BE INSERTED AFTER FIRST
rubrics_metrics.description: “EDITORS: TO COVER DEVELOPMENTS THE FOLLOWING MAY BE INSERTED AFTER FIRST SRAF STOCKHOLM SECOND LEAD ATTACK X X X PEACE. (THE NEW YORK TIMES SAID IT HAD RECEIVED WORD FROM ITS COPENHAGEN CORRESPONDENT...) AUTHORITATIVE QUARTERS X X X 2ND GRAF.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct editorial instruction: after the initial lead, insert second-lead material from correspondents (Stockholm, Copenhagen, etc.) and authoritative 'second graf' material; use correspondent dispatches to flesh out developments and follow-up facts as they arrive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence of immediate developments to report (enumerated items)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Within a few hours ... there came this sequence of events and reported events, piling one on the other in sensational style: 1. Reports that a German naval force of 125 armed ships... had moved out of the Baltic Sea into the passageway to the Kattegat and Skagerrak. 2. Reports of French intelligence agents that troops for some time had engaged in embarkation and disembarkation drills at Baltic ports. 3. The torpedoing and sinking by a British submarine of the German ‘mystery’ transport—the Rio De Janeiro—off the southeast coast of Norway with the loss of 300 of 500 German ... 4. ... 5. ... 6. All Norwegian lighthouses blacked out and radio stations shut down. 7. Four German warships supported by planes attempted to force their way through Oslo Fjord. 8. Oslo was under an air raid alarm throughout the early hours; communication was cut off except for 'State calls.' 9. Copenhagen, Denmark’s capital, was occupied by German troops. 10. Norway declared war ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this enumerated checklist as a template for what to include in breaking coverage — naval movements, intelligence indications, sinkings, communication blackouts, air raids, occupations of capitals, declarations of war. Report each numbered item with sourcing and timestamps where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include official government/military communiques and statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples in text: German communique: “The high command of the German Army announces that in order to counteract the actions against Denmark and Norway... the German Army has taken these two countries ‘under its protection.’” Also: statements from Norwegian Foreign Minister, State Department releases, British Foreign Office promises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give prominence to official communiques from involved governments and militaries; quote them verbatim when possible and indicate issuing authority and time. Contrast conflicting official claims (e.g., German 'protection' vs. Norwegian protest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Report military actions in land/sea/air detail (landings, naval entries, air raids, minefields, sinkings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Page reports: German troops landed at Moss and Oslo Fjord (2,000 soldiers); four German warships forcing Oslo Fjord; Nazi bombers roaring overhead; British mine-laying in Norwegian territorial waters; torpedoing/sinking of transports (Rio De Janeiro); reports of ships sunk at Narvik.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe mode of attack (land/sea/air), numbers landed, ship types involved, mine-laying activity, known sinkings and tonnage, and locations (ports/fjords). Distinguish between reported, confirmed, and unconfirmed military actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include diplomatic/consular telegrams and eyewitness diplomatic reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: “The American Minister to Oslo, Mrs. J. Borden Harriman, telegraphed to the Department of State tonight that the Foreign Minister has informed her that the Norwegians fired on four German warships... and that Norway is at war with Germany.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use communications from ministers, consuls and embassy staff as timely official eyewitness reports; attribute clearly and indicate how they reached the newsroom (telegraph, radio).

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe strategic/geographic context and motives (Skagerrak/Kattegat, Swedish iron ore, key ports)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article explains: “The Skagerrak... is the key to the Baltic... Swedish iron ore moving down the Norwegian coast to Germany was the smoldering fuse which set off the bombshell...” Background sections (Key to Baltic, Battle of Jutland history) provide strategic context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concise background explaining why the region is strategically important (sea lanes, ore shipments, minefields), including geographic names and historical precedents to help readers understand motives and implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Note communications disruption and censorship (telephone, radio, lighthouses, blackout)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports: telephone communication with Oslo cut off; 'we cannot reach Oslo' from operators; all Norwegian lighthouses blacked out; radio stations shut down; news enveloped by a 'screen of censorship.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report any disruptions to communications, blackouts and censorship; explain their effect on verification of reports and warn readers that some information may be delayed or controlled by authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute to multiple news agencies and local sources
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece cites Reuters, Associated Press (A.P.), the British Press Association, DNB (German news agency), Oslo radio, British Foreign Office and 'authoritative quarters.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute each claim to its source (agency, radio, government official) and indicate when reports conflict or are unconfirmed. Use multiple independent sources when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide human-interest details and casualty/rescue reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: first Canadian casualty Julien Durupt arriving in New York minus an eye; ship sinking off Lillesand with possibly 200 lost, rescue craft saved survivors; survivor counts and recovered bodies from various sinkings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include personal stories, survivor accounts and casualty/rescue numbers to humanize the story, but label unconfirmed casualty figures and provide sourcing for counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise chronology, times and quantified details (times, troop counts, ship tonnages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article gives specific times and numbers: 'Oslo surrendered at 4 P.M. today (10 A.M. New York time),' 'Two-thousand German soldiers were landed,' ship tonnages (e.g., 5,261-ton Rio De Janeiro), and times of communiques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where available, include timestamps, troop numbers, ship sizes and other quantifiable details; these improve clarity but must be sourced and caveated if unverified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flag possible propaganda/conflicting narratives and present denials/protests
rubrics_metrics.description: The article juxtaposes German claims of 'protection' and occupation without incident with Norwegian protests and reports of resistance and denial (Hamar government denying resignation), and notes 'Ominously behind a general screen of censorship...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When official narratives differ, present each side and note denials and protests; warn readers about possible propaganda and the difficulty of verification under wartime censorship.
